analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue federal agents who violate their constitutional rights for money damages.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 37 Democratic cosponsors, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since November 2025 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Supreme Court has ruled that people harmed by federal officers, such as Border Patrol or other federal agents, generally cannot sue those officers for money damages when their constitutional rights are violated, because Congress never passed a law creating that remedy. This bill closes that gap with a single sentence: it amends the existing civil-rights law that lets people sue state officials (42 U.S.C. 1983) so it also covers people acting under federal authority. A person beaten, detained, or otherwise abused by a federal agent could then sue that agent in court, just as they can sue a state or local officer today.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who suffer constitutional violations at the hands of federal officers — for example, people subjected to excessive force, unlawful searches or detention by Border Patrol, ICE, the FBI, or other federal agents. Today, after decades of Supreme Court rulings narrowing the judge-made 'Bivens' remedy, most of them have no way to recover damages; this bill would give them the same right to sue that exists against state and local officials [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Amends 42 U.S.C. 1983 so the civil remedy that already exists against state and local officials who violate constitutional rights also applies to people acting under federal authority [S2].

Would restore a damages remedy for constitutional violations by federal officers, which the Supreme Court has largely refused to recognize on its own, leaving most victims of federal officer misconduct without compensation [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Federal officers and, in practice, the federal agencies that indemnify them (pay judgments on their behalf) would bear the cost of damages in lawsuits, plus the cost of defending those suits. Law enforcement groups argue this exposes agents to personal liability for split-second decisions and could raise insurance and legal costs for agencies.

drawbacks.text: Officers personally named in suits would face the burden of litigation even when agencies ultimately pay, and agencies would face higher damages and defense costs; supporters of current law argue fear of personal liability can make officers hesitant to act forcefully in dangerous situations [S2].

A single-sentence extension of a Reconstruction-era statute resolves the policy with broad strokes; critics would prefer Congress to write detailed rules covering which federal roles can be sued, what defenses apply, and how agencies handle payments [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the upside is real: it creates a path to compensation and deterrence against federal officer misconduct that does not exist today for most situations. The costs fall on federal agencies and officers through litigation and damages, which is the mechanism that creates deterrence, but there is little protection in the bill against lawsuits over judgment calls in dangerous situations. The design is blunt, but the current alternative — no remedy at all for most federal officer abuses — leaves victims with nothing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee when introduced and the committee has taken no action on it since; no vote has occurred in either chamber.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the Bivens Act of 2025 on November 18, 2025, joined by 14 original cosponsors including Rep. Jamie Raskin [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote since [S4].
All 37 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on [S3].
The bill's entire operative change is one amendment: inserting 'of the United States or' into 42 U.S.C. 1983 so federal actors are covered alongside state actors [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies and their officers remain, for now, largely shielded from private damages suits for constitutional violations, because the committee has not moved the bill.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (Border Patrol, ICE, FBI, federal prison officers)
industries.note: The bill would make federal officers subject to private damages suits for constitutional violations, ending the practical immunity most federal officers enjoy after Supreme Court narrowing of the Bivens remedy. Agencies would pay or indemnify judgments, and the threat of suits would create financial accountability that does not exist today [S2].

These groups have fought officer personal liability at every level of government, and the bill would extend that liability to federal agents, a major expansion beyond state and local police accountability rules.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, a referral-only status, and a Judiciary Committee majority that has shown no interest, the realistic path is that the bill sits without a vote for the rest of the 119th Congress. A change in committee interest or a high-profile federal abuse case could produce a hearing, but passage would require either Democratic control of the House or significant Republican support that does not currently exist.
